Cut Cylinder

Game: This shows the shape you get where a flat sheet cuts through a cylinder.
How to play: Drag the dots or slide the controls to tilt and move the sheet. Press a shape button for a ready-made cut.
30° 2.0
Look for the math

A flat sheet can meet a round cylinder in a surprising small set of curves. No matter how you tilt or slide it, you only ever see one of three kinds of cut.

What the page claims

The original page says: “The possible sections are circles, ellipses, and parallel lines that may coalesce.” The logic test checks this over every whole-degree tilt and every whole-unit position, plus thousands of other settings: it holds. Two details the sentence leaves out: a sheet completely past the cylinder gives no cut at all, and an oval can be trimmed short by the cylinder's flat ends.

tilt = 0° → circle
0° < tilt < 90° → ellipse
tilt = 90° → two parallel lines, or one when the sheet just touches

Why those are the only shapes

Put the cylinder's axis along x and let its round side be y² + z² = 6². A plane whose normal leans by β from the axis, at distance d from the centre, meets it where

(u cosβ + d sinβ)² + v² = 6²

Here u and v are coordinates inside the sheet. For β < 90° this is a stretched circle: an ellipse with half-widths 6/cosβ and 6. At β = 0 the two half-widths are both 6, a circle. At β = 90° the u term drops out and v = ±√(6² − d²): two lines running along the axis. Their gap shrinks to zero when |d| = 6, so the two lines become one — the coalescence the page mentions.

What changed from the Java applet

The applet drew a Java 3D cylinder of radius 6 and height 18 and a square sheet of side 20; you rotated, slid and zoomed them with the mouse. Its radio buttons chose separate or combined motion and a transparent or opaque sheet. This port keeps those two choices and the cylinder's size, but trades the 3D mouse gestures for a side view, a face-on view, two draggable dots and sliders. In the flat view, “combined” only changes the label: the picture already shows the sheet's position relative to the cylinder, which is all that decides the cut. The applet never named the curve; the names here come from its page.

Press Two lines, then slide the sheet slowly outward. Watch the two lines move together and become one at Just touching.
